entry: American multinational confectionery, food and beverage company based in [[Chicago]]. Mondelez has annual revenue of about $38.5 billion and operates in approximately 160 countries, and it ranked No. 108 in the 2021 Fortune 500 list. The company traces its origins to Kraft Foods Inc., founded in Chicago in 1923. In 2012 Kraft Foods was renamed Mondelez and kept its snack food business, while its North American grocery business was spun off as Kraft Foods Group. The name combines the Latin *mundus* ("world") with "delez", a derivative of "delicious". Its brands include [[Cadbury]], Milka, Toblerone, Oreo and Halls.

Spanish heist crime drama television series. Created by Álex Pina, it follows the Professor, who recruits a team of robbers for two long-prepared heists: one on the Royal Mint of Spain and one on the Bank of Spain. The story is told partly from the perspective of the robber Tokyo and relies on an unreliable narrator and flashbacks. It first aired on Antena 3 in 2017, and [[Netflix]] later expanded it into five parts released through 2021. Filmed in [[Madrid]], it won the International Emmy Award for Best Drama Series at the 46th International Emmy Awards. The spin-off *Berlin* was released in 2023.

Series of military campaigns that created the largest contiguous empire in history. The conquests took place during the 13th and 14th centuries and produced the [[Mongol Empire]] (1206–1368), which by 1260 covered a significant portion of [[Eurasia]], stretching from the Pacific to [[Central Europe]]. As the empire began to fragment after 1260, conflict with Eastern European states continued for centuries. Mongols ruled [[China]] into the 14th century under the [[Yuan dynasty]], and Mongol rule in Persia lasted into the 15th century under the [[Timurid Empire]], while the later [[Mughal Empire]] survived in the Indian subcontinent into the 19th century. Earlier nomadic armies relied on mounted archers but were weak in siege warfare and lacked discipline. The reforms of [[Genghis Khan]] addressed these weaknesses, and the Mongol army became one of the most formidable forces in history.

Landlocked country in East Asia. It is bordered by Russia to the north and China to the south, and it covers 1,564,116 sq km (603,909 sq mi), making it the second-largest landlocked nation after [[Kazakhstan]]. With a population of 3.5 million, it is the world's most sparsely populated sovereign state, and roughly half of its people live in the capital, [[Ulaanbaatar]]. The territory was ruled by various nomadic empires before [[Genghis Khan]] founded the [[Mongol Empire]] in 1206. The [[Qing dynasty]] absorbed the country in the 17th century. Mongolia declared independence in 1911 and gained actual independence from the Republic of China in 1921. It became a satellite state of the [[Soviet Union]], and after the 1990 democratic revolution a 1992 constitution established a multiparty system and a market economy. Mahayana Buddhism is the majority religion, practiced by 51.7% of the population.

East Asian ethnic group native to [[Mongolia]], China and parts of southern [[Siberia]]. Mongols are the principal member of the Mongolic peoples. The Oirats and Buryats are classified either as distinct ethnolinguistic groups or as subgroups of the Mongols. They speak Mongolian dialects. Mongols live in China's Inner Mongolia and 11 other autonomous territories. The word "Mongol" first appeared in the Chinese *Old Book of Tang* in the mid-10th century, describing a Shiwei tribe. In the 13th century it became an umbrella term for Mongolic-speaking tribes united under [[Genghis Khan]]. The Mongols of the [[Mongol Empire]] were known in Europe as "Tatars".

Small terrestrial carnivorous [[Mammal|mammal]] of the family Herpestidae, found in Africa and Asia. The family has two subfamilies: the Herpestinae, with 23 living species native to southern Europe, Africa and Asia, and the Mungotinae, with 11 species native to Africa. Herpestidae originated about 21.8 ± 3.6 million years ago in the Early Miocene. Mongooses have long faces and bodies, short legs, long tapering tails and nonretractable claws. Their head-to-body length ranges from 24 to 58 cm, and they weigh from 320 g to 5 kg. Their diets consist mainly of insects, rodents, reptiles and birds. Mongooses are one of at least four mammalian taxa with mutations in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that protect against snake venom. Some species are kept as pets to control vermin, and a large introduced population lives on [[Hawaii]].

Yugoslav-born American tennis player. Seles was ranked world No. 1 in women's singles for 178 weeks and won 53 singles titles, including nine [[Grand Slam (tennis)|major titles]], eight as a teenager. In 1990 she became the youngest-ever French Open champion, at 16. On April 30, 1993, an obsessed fan of her rival [[Steffi Graf]] stabbed her in the back during a match. She did not play for over two years, struggling with depression and an eating disorder. After returning in 1995, she won her ninth major at the 1996 Australian Open. She was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in 2009.

Philosophical view that reality is ultimately one kind of thing. The term attributes oneness to a concept such as existence and is used primarily in [[Philosophy]], where it sometimes overlaps with nondualism. Priority monism holds that all things derive from a distinct source, as in Neoplatonism, where everything derives from the One. Existence monism holds that strictly only the universe exists. Substance monism explains existing things by a single substance, such as matter or mind, while dual-aspect monism treats the mental and the physical as two aspects of one substance. Neutral monism holds that the fundamental nature of reality is neither mental nor physical. The term was introduced in the 18th century by Christian von Wolff in *Logic* (1728). [[Baruch Spinoza]] argued that "God or Nature" is the only substance of the universe.

Lizard of the genus *Varanus*, the only living genus in the family Varanidae. About 94 species are recognized. They are native to Africa, Asia and Oceania, and one invasive species is also found in the southern United States. Monitor lizards have long necks, powerful tails and claws. Living species range from 20 cm (7.9 in) in length to over 3 m (10 ft) in the case of the [[Komodo dragon]]. Most are terrestrial, though many are arboreal or semiaquatic. Most are carnivorous, eating small reptiles, fish, birds, insects, small mammals and eggs, and a few also eat fruit and vegetation.

Simian primate other than an ape. Traditionally, all simians except apes are called monkeys, and apes are deep within the same family tree. The Old World monkeys ([[Old World monkey|Catarrhini]]), named by Étienne Geoffroy in 1812, are native to Africa and Asia. The New World monkeys (Platyrrhini) are native to Central and South America and are thought to have reached South America by ocean. Many species are arboreal, though some, such as [[Baboon|baboons]], live mainly on the ground. Most are diurnal, and monkeys are generally considered intelligent, especially the Old World monkeys. Simians diverged from [[Tarsier|tarsiers]] some 70 million years ago. Some species, such as the [[Rhesus macaque|rhesus macaque]], serve as models for human physiology in biomedical research.

Fictional character and protagonist of the *One Piece* [[Manga|manga]] series. Created by Eiichiro Oda, Luffy is the captain of the Straw Hat Crew. After eating a Devil Fruit as a child, he gains a rubber body, used in attacks such as the Gum-Gum Pistol. At 17 he sets sail to find the treasure One Piece and become King of the Pirates. He becomes one of the Four Emperors of the Sea. He appears in most episodes and films of the anime and in several [[Video game|video games]]. His critical reception has been largely positive, and he has placed first in every popularity poll.

Clade of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] whose seeds contain only one embryonic leaf, or cotyledon. Monocotyledons, or monocots, are contrasted with dicotyledons, which have two cotyledons. The APG IV system recognizes the monocots as a monophyletic group without assigning it a rank. Monocots are of major economic importance and make up a majority of the plant biomass used in agriculture. Crops such as dates, onions, garlic, [[Rice]], [[Wheat]], [[Maize]] and [[Sugarcane]] are monocots. The grasses cover over 40% of Earth's land area. [[Orchid|Orchids]], [[Tulip|tulips]], daffodils and lilies are common houseplants. The group comprises about 60,000 to 85,000 species, roughly one-quarter of angiosperm diversity.

Form of dyadic relationship with one partner at any one time. The term, derived from Greek for "one marriage", has genetic, sexual, social and marital meanings. Biologists distinguish social, sexual and genetic monogamy, which do not always coincide, and serial monogamy describes successive exclusive relationships. It contrasts with non-monogamy such as [[Polygamy|polygamy]] or [[Polyamory|polyamory]]. Monogamy in humans varies across cultures. A minority of societies are strictly monogamous, while many others practice serial monogamy or tolerate extramarital sex. Genetic monogamy is relatively unstudied and is often contradicted by evidence of extrapair paternity. Human monogamy likely evolved from factors such as the need for paternal care, together with cultural developments such as [[Agriculture|agriculture]], property inheritance and religious norms.

Market structure in which a single firm is the only supplier of a good or service. A monopoly lacks economic competition and viable substitutes, which allows a price well above marginal cost. In law, a monopoly is a business with significant market power, and size is not a defining characteristic. Monopolies may form through mergers, arise naturally where production is resource-intensive, or be established by a government, as with [[Patent|patents]] and [[Copyright|copyrights]]. A monopsony, with a single buyer, is a related situation, and a monopoly differs from a cartel, in which several providers coordinate. Many jurisdictions use [[Competition (economics)|competition]] laws to restrict monopolies, although holding a dominant position is often not illegal in itself, and certain abusive behaviors can be sanctioned.

Multiplayer economics-themed [[Board game|board game]]. Players roll two [[Dice|dice]] to move around the board, buying and trading properties and railroads and developing them with houses and hotels. They collect rent from opponents and aim to drive them into bankruptcy. Players receive a salary when they pass "Go", and Chance and Community Chest cards and tax squares can also gain or cost money. The game is derived from *The Landlord's Game*, created in 1903 by Lizzie Magie to show that an economy rewarding individuals was better than one in which monopolies held all the wealth. Parker Brothers first published the game in 1935, and it was absorbed into Hasbro in 1991. It has been licensed in more than 113 countries and had sold an estimated 275 million copies by 2015.

Form of urban rail transit with vehicles on or suspended from a single rail or beam. Monorails typically provide intermediate capacity, greater than [[Tram|trams]] and less than heavy metro systems. Two principal types exist: straddle-beam monorails, in which vehicles ride atop a concrete or steel beam, and suspended monorails, in which vehicles hang beneath the guideway. The straddle-beam design descends from the ALWEG system of the 1950s and dominates modern installations. The Wuppertal Schwebebahn, in service since 1901, is the oldest monorail in operation. Tokyo Monorail has carried over 1.5 billion passengers since 1964. [[Chongqing]] Rail Transit in China operates the world's largest and busiest monorail system, and its Line 3 carries over 680,000 passengers per day. Monorails are most often used in large cities, at airports and in theme parks.

Sodium salt of glutamic acid used as a flavor enhancer. It occurs naturally in some foods, including tomatoes and [[Cheese|cheese]], and intensifies the [[Umami|umami]] flavor of food. The Japanese biochemist Kikunae Ikeda first extracted it in 1908 while trying to duplicate the savory taste of kombu, an edible [[Seaweed|seaweed]] used in Japanese broth. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has designated it generally recognized as safe. The popular belief that it causes headaches, known as Chinese restaurant syndrome, is not supported by several blinded studies at normal concentrations. The European Union permits it subject to quantitative limits and designates it E621.

Belief in only one deity, or God. Monotheism differs from henotheism, which worships one god without denying that others may be worshipped, and from monolatry, which recognizes many gods but worships only one. Exclusive monotheism holds that God is a singular existence, while inclusive and pluriform monotheism regard multiple divine forms as extensions of the same God. Monotheism characterizes [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]], together with early offshoots such as Samaritanism and the Druze faith. Other monotheistic traditions include the Atenism of ancient Egypt, [[Zoroastrianism]], Manichaeism, [[Deism]] and [[Sikhism]]. Elements of monotheistic thought are also found in ancient Chinese religion, Tengrism and Yahwism.

Egg-laying [[Mammal|mammal]] of the order Monotremata. The five living species are the [[Platypus]] and four species of [[Echidna|echidnas]]. Female monotremes nurse their young with milk, like other mammals, but they differ from other living mammals in brain, jaw, digestive and reproductive structures. All living species are native to [[Australia]] and [[New Guinea]], though monotremes were also present in southern South America during the Late Cretaceous and Paleocene. The name, from Greek *monos* ("single") and *trema* ("hole"), refers to the [[Cloaca|cloaca]]. They lay one to three small eggs, which incubate for about 10 to 12 days, and the young, called puggles, nurse for several months.

U.S. foreign policy position opposing foreign interference in the Western Hemisphere. President [[James Monroe]] first articulated the doctrine on December 2, 1823, in his seventh annual message to Congress; it was not named after him until 1850. Monroe declared that the New World and Old World were separate spheres of influence, and that European efforts to control or influence sovereign states in the Americas would be viewed as a threat to U.S. security. The United States, in turn, would not interfere with existing European colonies. Because the United States lacked a credible navy and army, the doctrine was largely ignored, though the United Kingdom partly enforced it. The United States enforced it itself early in the 20th century. After 1898 it was reinterpreted as promoting multilateralism and non-intervention, and in 1933 Franklin D. Roosevelt affirmed this view by co-founding the [[Organization of American States]].

Capital and largest city of [[Liberia]], on the Atlantic coast. Founded in April 1822 by the American Colonization Society as a settlement for free people of color from the [[United States]], the city stands on Cape Mesurado on land traditionally held by the Vai people. It was named for President [[James Monroe]], a supporter of the colonization effort. As of the 2022 census, it had 1,761,032 residents, and its metropolitan area, including Montserrado and Margibi counties, had 2,225,911 inhabitants, or 33.5% of Liberia's population. Monrovia is the nation's economic, financial and cultural center, and its economy centers on its harbor and the seat of government. The Freeport of Monrovia is the country's largest and main port.

Seasonal change in atmospheric circulation and precipitation. Traditionally a seasonal reversing wind, the term now describes changes associated with the annual latitudinal oscillation of the [[Intertropical Convergence Zone]]. It usually refers to the rainy phase of the pattern, although a dry phase also exists, and it can describe locally heavy but short-term rains. The major monsoon systems are the West African, South Asian–Australian, North American and South American monsoons. The term was first used in English in British India for the large seasonal winds that blew from the [[Bay of Bengal]] and the [[Arabian Sea]] in the southwest, bringing heavy rainfall.

Imaginary creature, often dangerous and grotesque, found in literature, folklore and religion. Monsters are usually capable of killing or causing destruction, and they threaten the social or moral order of the human world. Animal monsters lie outside the moral order, while human monsters, such as [[Medusa]] and her Gorgon sisters, were never fully human or have lost their humanity, as with werewolves and Frankenstein's monster. Some monsters are depicted as misunderstood or friendly, and others as mischievous or large and clumsy enough to cause unintentional damage. Monsters predate written history. Well-known fictional examples include [[Dracula]], werewolves, [[Vampire|vampires]], [[Demon|demons]], reanimated mummies and [[Zombie|zombies]]. In Greek myth, the [[Minotaur]], a man with a bull's head, was born after a punishment sent by [[Poseidon]].

Highest mountain in the [[Alps]], on the Franco-Italian border. It rises 4,807.3 m (15,771.9 ft) above sea level and is the highest mountain in Europe outside the [[Caucasus Mountains]]. It is the second-most prominent mountain in Europe, after [[Mount Elbrus]]. The mountain gives its name to the Mont Blanc massif, which straddles [[France]], [[Italy]] and [[Switzerland]]. Ownership of the summit area has long been disputed between France and Italy. The massif is popular for hiking, climbing and skiing, and the most common route to the summit, the Goûter Route, typically takes two days. Michel-Gabriel Paccard and Jacques Balmat first reached the summit on August 8, 1786. The 11.6 km Mont Blanc Tunnel, built between 1957 and 1965, runs beneath the mountain.

Tidal island and commune in [[Normandy]], France. The island lies about one kilometer off the northwestern coast, at the mouth of the Couesnon River. Its abbey drew pilgrims, who could reach it at low tide, and the tide made it defensible. The island remained unconquered during the [[Hundred Years' War]], and a small garrison repelled an English attack in 1433. [[Louis XI]] turned it into a prison, and the abbey continued to serve as a prison during the *Ancien Régime*. The island and its bay were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, and more than three million people visit each year.
